reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Characterised by recurrent self-limiting episodes of intrahepatic cholestasis with intense pruritus and jaundice separated by symptom-free intervals
It is allelic with progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis, involving milder variants of the same genes: ATP8B1 in type 1 and ABCB11 in type 2
As with the low-GGT PFIC subtypes, the gamma-glutamyl transferase is characteristically normal or low despite marked cholestasis
Attacks may be triggered by intercurrent infection, hormonal changes, or drugs, and can last weeks to months before resolving
By definition it does not cause permanent liver damage or progress to cirrhosis, distinguishing it from progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis
The prodrome of malaise and pruritus precedes a cholestatic phase with raised bile acids and conjugated bilirubin but preserved synthetic function
Management is supportive during attacks, focusing on relief of pruritus and nutrition, with no need for transplantation in classic disease
reference.pathophysiology: Benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis arises from partial-function mutations in the same canalicular transport proteins implicated in progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis: the aminophospholipid flippase FIC1 (ATP8B1) in type 1 and the bile salt export pump BSEP (ABCB11) in type 2. Because residual transporter function is retained, hepatocyte bile acid secretion is only intermittently impaired, typically when an additional stress such as infection, hormonal change, or a drug tips the balance. During an episode, bile acids and conjugated bilirubin accumulate and cholestasis with pruritus develops, but between episodes bile flow normalises and the liver recovers without lasting structural injury. The normal or low gamma-glutamyl transferase reflects that, as in the corresponding PFIC subtypes, the underlying lesion does not damage the bile duct epithelium.
additionalDifferentials: Primary biliary cholangitis and other cholestatic disorders
additionalInvestigations: Serum bile acids, bilirubin fractions, and gamma-glutamyl transferase during an episode
Liver enzymes and synthetic function showing recovery between attacks
Imaging to exclude extrahepatic biliary obstruction
Molecular genetic testing of ATP8B1 and ABCB11
Liver biopsy in atypical cases showing bland cholestasis without progressive fibrosis
Review of drug, hormonal, and infective triggers
redFlags: Failure of an episode to resolve or evidence of progressive fibrosis, suggesting a PFIC phenotype rather than benign disease
Coagulopathy or synthetic dysfunction, which are not expected in classic disease
Severe intractable pruritus with major impact on sleep and quality of life
Features of biliary obstruction requiring exclusion of an alternative cause
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign with a normal life expectancy; episodes are self-limiting and, by definition, do not progress to chronic liver disease or cirrhosis, although attacks can be prolonged and debilitating during the cholestatic phase.
pitfalls: Investigating recurrent cholestasis repeatedly for biliary obstruction without considering an inherited cause
Failing to recognise the shared genetic basis and low-GGT pattern linking it to progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis
Assuming progression to cirrhosis and pursuing transplantation inappropriately in classic disease
Overlooking identifiable triggers such as drugs or hormonal changes
Undertreating disabling pruritus during acute episodes
references: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
management: Manage episodes symptomatically, as attacks are self-limiting and do not require treatment aimed at halting disease progression
Control cholestatic pruritus with a bile acid sequestrant such as cholestyramine, adding rifampicin or ursodeoxycholic acid for refractory itch
Consider nasobiliary drainage or plasma-based therapies for severe, prolonged and disabling cholestatic attacks
Supplement fat-soluble vitamins during prolonged cholestatic phases complicated by malabsorption
Identify and remove precipitating triggers such as intercurrent infection, hormonal agents and offending drugs
Reassure regarding the benign course while monitoring liver biochemistry to confirm recovery between attacks and exclude progression
Offer genetic counselling given the heritable ATP8B1 and ABCB11 basis, with family testing where appropriate

flowcharts.title: Diagnosis and management of benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis

nodes.text: Recurrent intense pruritus and jaundice, with symptom-free intervals between episodes
Red flag: episode not resolving, fibrosis, coagulopathy or features of obstruction?
Escalate: consider PFIC; exclude obstruction and assess for fibrosis on biopsy
Measure bile acids, bilirubin fractions and GGT during an episode
Imaging of the biliary tree; ATP8B1 and ABCB11 genetic testing
Obstruction excluded, with bland cholestasis and normal GGT?
Remove triggers; control pruritus with cholestyramine, adding rifampicin if refractory
No: consider PFIC or another cause of cholestasis; specialist review
Monitor biochemistry for recovery; genetic counselling and family testing
Benign course without cirrhosis; episodes are self-limiting but can be prolonged
